result: ABC transporters, including TmrAB, are a large family of primary active transporters with established roles in multiple diseases and physiological processes. TmrAB from Thermus thermophilus is structurally and functionally homologous to TAP and is suitable for mechanistic studies due to temperature-dependent conformational accessibility.
evaluation: Claims C1, C4-C12 provide well-established background information about ABC transporters and TmrAB, supported by appropriate citations to prior research. These claims establish the biological and experimental context for the study.

result: Multiple catalytic models exist for ABC transporters, all linking substrate translocation to ATP-driven conformational transitions. Prior structural and functional studies on TmrAB have elucidated the conformational landscape and demonstrated unidirectional substrate export along a single ATP-induced conformational switch.
evaluation: Claims C13-C16 summarize established mechanistic models and prior work on TmrAB, appropriately cited. These claims provide the mechanistic framework and identify the knowledge gap that the current study addresses.

result: Macrocyclic peptides (CPs) are next-generation pharmaceutical compounds with advantages over conventional drugs. The RaPID system enables identification of synthetic CPs with unnatural amino acids against target proteins and has been successfully applied to multiple protein targets.
evaluation: Claims C17-C23 provide well-documented background on macrocyclic peptides and the RaPID selection system, supported by appropriate citations. These establish the methodological foundation for the study.

result: A library of ~10^12 macrocyclic peptides was generated using the RaPID system with head-to-side chain cyclization. After five rounds of selection against TmrAEQB in lipid nanodiscs, four abundant macrocyclic peptides (CP6, CP12, CP13, CP14) were identified, constituting 41% of the final pool.
evaluation: Claims C27-C30 describe the library generation and selection process with appropriate experimental detail. The enrichment data (Figure 1C) and deep sequencing results support the identification of the four lead CPs.

result: All four CPs bind TmrAB with nanomolar affinity (KD 20-50 nM) in a specific, conformation-dependent manner. The CPs form kinetically stable, stoichiometric complexes with TmrAB and can be used for affinity purification of the transporter.
evaluation: Claims C31-C37 are well-supported by multiple complementary techniques including fluorescence polarization (Figure 2A,B), affinity capture (Figure 2C,D), gel filtration (Figure 2—supplement 1), SDS disruption experiments, and native MS (Figure 2E). The convergent evidence from multiple methods strongly supports these binding characteristics.

result: All CPs completely block ATP hydrolysis to autohydrolysis levels and are not transported substrates. CP6F and CP12F completely block peptide translocation, while CP13F and CP14F cause partial inhibition.
evaluation: Claims C38-C41 are supported by ATPase assays (Figure 3B) and transport assays (Figure 3C,D). The differential inhibition patterns between CP6/CP12 (complete block) and CP13/CP14 (partial inhibition) are clearly demonstrated and form the basis for mechanistic classification.

result: CPs are allosteric inhibitors that do not compete with substrate binding and have minimal effects on ATP binding, while completely blocking ATP hydrolysis and substrate translocation.
evaluation: Claims C42-C46 are supported by competition binding experiments (Figure 4A,B) and ATP binding assays (Figure 4C). The lack of competition with substrates and minimal ATP binding effects, combined with complete inhibition of hydrolysis and transport, clearly establish an allosteric mechanism.

result: CP6F and CP12F preferentially bind the IF conformation and block the IF-to-OF transition by preventing nucleotide occlusion. CP13F and CP14F preferentially bind the OF conformation and stabilize a pre-hydrolysis state by promoting ATP occlusion while blocking hydrolysis to ADP.
evaluation: Claims C47-C52 are strongly supported by conformation-specific binding studies (Figure 5A,B and supplements) and nucleotide occlusion experiments (Figure 5C,D). The differential binding preferences and effects on nucleotide occlusion clearly distinguish two mechanistic classes of inhibitors.

result: Single-liposome transport assays demonstrate that CP13F and CP14F allow transport of 10-30 peptides per liposome along a single IF-to-OF switch, yielding a coupling ratio of 0.3-1.0 peptides per transporter. CP6F and CP12F completely prevent transport. The CPs bind from the cytosolic side.
evaluation: Claims C53-C56 are supported by single-liposome flow cytometry data (Figure 6A,B). The quantification is based on calibration curves (Figure 6—supplement 1) and accounts for the number of transporters per liposome. The inference about cytosolic binding (C56) is reasonable given membrane impermeability of CPs.

result: Time-course and two-cycle transport experiments show that CP13F causes conformational arrest after a single turnover, while CP14F allows slow turnover. CP13 and CP14 stabilize a pre-hydrolysis state allowing single-turnover translocation along the IF-to-OF switch.
evaluation: Claims C57-C62 are supported by time-course transport data (Figure 6C,D) and two-cycle experiments (Figure 6E). The differential behavior between CP13F (single turnover arrest) and CP14F (slow turnover) is clearly demonstrated and mechanistically consistent with the nucleotide occlusion data.

result: Macrocyclic peptides can arrest TmrAB at different stages of the ATP-induced IF-to-OF switch that drives substrate transport. These inhibitors stabilize states distinct from vanadate-trapped states and demonstrate for the first time in a wild-type ABC transporter that substrate translocation is driven along a single IF-to-OF switch triggered by ATP binding.
evaluation: Claims C63, C64, C86, C87 represent the major conclusions of the study, well-supported by the collective experimental evidence including conformation-specific binding, nucleotide occlusion, and single-liposome transport assays. The distinction from vanadate-trapped states is supported by comparison of nucleotide occlusion patterns (Figure 5C,D).

result: CPs selected against TmrAEQB in nanodiscs bind wild-type TmrAB in various lipid models and display inhibitory activity despite selection based on binding alone. The enrichment patterns reflect the conformational preferences of the CPs and the selection conditions (4°C favoring IF state).
evaluation: Claims C68-C71, C75 are supported by the binding data across different systems and deep sequencing results (Figure 1C). The correlation between enrichment and conformational preference is logical and consistent with the known temperature-dependent conformational behavior of TmrAB.

result: Unlike CPs against other transporters (aCAP, MATE transporters), the CPs in this study target TmrAB from the cytosolic side. The CPs are enriched in aliphatic and aromatic amino acids, which could indicate membrane interactions.
evaluation: Claim C72 is an inference based on membrane impermeability and comparison with other studies. Claim C74 is speculative about potential membrane interactions based on sequence composition. While the cytosolic targeting is reasonable, the membrane interaction hypothesis lacks direct experimental support.

result: Recent structural studies have expanded understanding of ABC transporter conformational space and mechanistic models. Prior work demonstrated unidirectional transport along a single IF-to-OF switch for a catalytically reduced TmrAB variant, but whether this applies to wild-type transporters and the nature of energy coupling remained open questions.
evaluation: Claims C76-C81 appropriately summarize recent advances and identify the knowledge gaps that motivate the current study. These are well-supported by citations and accurately frame the scientific context.

result: CP13F and CP14F stabilize wild-type TmrAB in a pre-hydrolysis state distinct from vanadate-trapped states. The hypothesis that these CPs allow IF-to-OF transition but block OF-to-IF return is tested and supported. The coupling ratio under single-turnover conditions is substantially higher than in multiple-turnover steady-state approaches.
evaluation: Claims C83-C85 are supported by nucleotide occlusion data (Figure 5C,D), single-liposome transport data (Figure 6B), and comparison with prior steady-state measurements. The hypothesis (C84) is explicitly tested and validated by the experimental results.

result: Macrocyclic peptides are powerful tools for stabilizing protein conformers, mimicking antibody CDRs with expanded chemical diversity through unnatural amino acids. ABC transporter inhibitors exploit various mechanisms including substrate competition, conformational arrest, and ATP hydrolysis inhibition.
evaluation: Claims C65-C67, C82 provide well-established background on CPs and ABC transporter inhibitors, appropriately cited. These contextualize the approach and findings of the study.

result: Future approaches using conformation-selective compounds with single-liposome or single-molecule techniques will be essential for uncovering unexplored aspects of membrane translocation complexes.
evaluation: Claim C88 is a reasonable forward-looking statement based on the demonstrated utility of the approach in this study. It appropriately suggests future research directions.

result: High-affinity peptidic macrocycles bind conformationally selective to TmrAB and display potent multimode inhibitory effects. Two mechanistically distinct CP inhibitor classes arrest the ABC transporter either before (IF state) or after (OF state) ATP-binding induced substrate translocation.
evaluation: Claims C2, C3, C24-C26 represent the core findings summarized in the abstract. These are well-supported by the comprehensive experimental data including binding studies, inhibition assays, conformation-specific binding, nucleotide occlusion, and transport experiments presented throughout the manuscript.
